title: Facilitate behaviour change and innovation in extension

lessons.title: How farmers adopt new practices
lessons.html:
Behaviour change is the goal of extension

Extension is successful only when people do something differently: a smallholder plants drought-tolerant maize, a stockman starts keeping dosing records, a co-operative begins grading its tomatoes before sending them to the fresh produce market. Knowledge alone does not guarantee change. A practitioner must understand how and why people adopt innovations.

The adoption process

Diffusion of innovations theory, associated with Everett Rogers, describes stages that an individual moves through:

  1. Awareness - hears about the innovation, for example at a farmers' day.
  2. Interest - looks for more information.
  3. Evaluation - weighs it against own situation and resources.
  4. Trial - tests it on a small scale, such as one camp or a few rows.
  5. Adoption - uses it fully and continues.

Adopter categories

People adopt at different speeds: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards. Early adopters are often respected local farmers; when they succeed, others follow. Labelling someone a laggard is unhelpful. Late adopters often have good reasons, such as limited cash, high risk or lack of land tenure.

Characteristics of the innovation

  • Relative advantage - is it clearly better, in rand and in effort?
  • Compatibility - does it fit culture, existing equipment and farming calendar?
  • Complexity - is it easy to understand and use?
  • Trialability - can it be tested on a small scale?
  • Observability - can neighbours see the results?

An innovation that scores well on these five is far more likely to spread. Your job is often to make the advantage visible and the trial easy.

lessons.title: Barriers and drivers of change
lessons.html:
Why people resist or embrace change

Behaviour is shaped by knowledge, attitudes, skills, resources and social pressure. A farmer may know that rotational grazing improves veld condition but still graze all animals in one camp because fencing is broken, cattle are shared among family members or there is fear of theft in distant camps.

Common barriers in South African settings

  • Limited access to credit, inputs and markets.
  • Insecure tenure on communal or land reform farms, which reduces long-term investment.
  • Risk from drought, disease outbreaks and price swings.
  • Traditional authority and family decision-making structures that the practitioner did not consult.
  • Past experience with projects that failed or with promises that were not kept.
  • Gender roles: women often do much of the farm work but may not control the income or attend meetings.

Drivers of change

  • A clear economic benefit, shown in the farmer's own figures.
  • Peer example from a trusted neighbour or study group.
  • Market requirements, for example a buyer demanding traceability or GLOBALG.A.P. certification.
  • Policy and regulation, such as the need to register dip and vaccination records under animal health schemes.
  • Personal motivation: pride, wanting children to farm, community recognition.

Diagnosing the real barrier

Use open questions and farm walks to find the true reason for non-adoption. Ask what the farmer would need to try the practice. Separate what the farmer cannot do (resource problem) from what the farmer does not want to do (attitude problem) and from what they do not know how to do (skill problem). Each requires a different response: linking to finance, building trust, or practical training. Never blame or shame farmers; it destroys the relationship.

lessons.title: Facilitating innovation in practice
lessons.html:
The practitioner as facilitator

Modern extension sees the practitioner as a facilitator of learning and innovation rather than an expert who hands down answers. Innovation often comes from combining research knowledge with farmers' own ideas. A farmer in the Eastern Cape who adapts a shade-net design for seedlings using local materials is innovating.

Facilitation methods

  • On-farm trials. Farmers compare the new practice with their usual practice side by side, and record results themselves.
  • Farmer field schools. A group meets regularly through a whole season to observe, discuss and decide.
  • Exchange visits. Taking farmers to see a successful neighbour or another district.
  • Innovation platforms. Bringing together farmers, buyers, input suppliers, researchers and officials to solve a shared problem.

A facilitation cycle

  1. Build trust and agree on the problem with the group.
  2. Explore options, including local knowledge.
  3. Plan a small trial with clear roles.
  4. Observe and measure results together.
  5. Reflect: what worked, what did not and why.
  6. Scale up what worked and share it through farmer-to-farmer learning.

Supporting change over time

Change is often not permanent after one season. Follow up, celebrate success publicly, and help early adopters become champions. Be honest when a practice does not work in a particular setting. Ensure that any recommended product is registered and used according to the label.

Key points

  • Adoption moves through awareness, interest, evaluation, trial and adoption.
  • Relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability influence uptake.
  • Find the real barrier: knowledge, skill, resources or attitude.
  • Facilitate through on-farm trials, field schools, exchange visits and platforms.
  • Follow up and use early adopters as local champions.
